strengths: Clear and well-motivated empirical observation: after GRPO post-training, MLLMs (LLaVA) exhibit gradient saliency on task-irrelevant background regions whereas text-only LLMs do not (Figures 2, 8; Appendix C.1), providing a plausible link between outcome-only rewards, spurious background correlations, and hallucination.

The causal framing is grounded in established theory (probability of sufficiency and necessity, PNS, from Pearl's framework), and the paper carefully positions itself against closely related work such as [73] and [75] (Appendix C.3), including differences in motivation, methodology, and evaluation setting.

The proposed causal completeness reward (token-level sufficiency via prefix-continuation rollouts, necessity via token masking) is a concrete, implementable mechanism integrated into the GRPO advantage, with pseudo-code and notational tables provided in the appendix.

Unusually broad experimental coverage: CHAIR/POPE/MME and GPT-4-assisted caption evaluation on four MLLM backbones, plus V*, HR-Bench, refCOCO variants, ReasonSeg, and multiple math/reasoning benchmarks; ablations of each reward component (Table 3), GRPO-variant plug-in experiments (DAPO, Dr. GRPO, GCPO; Table 9), decoding-mode comparisons (Table 8), implementation-path ablations (Table 10), and hyperparameter sensitivity for λ_s, λ_n, and H.
Explicit treatment of the efficiency trade-off (Figure 12) and offline rollout collection, acknowledging the cost of per-token causal scoring rather than hiding it.
weaknesses: The causal machinery is largely heuristic rather than faithful to the stated formalism. Eq. 6 applies an indicator function that zeroes out non-improving tokens, and the necessity score (Eq. 7) uses a single deterministic decoding rather than the multiple-sample counterfactual averaging that Definition 3.1 specifies. The resulting scores are ad-hoc proxies for PNS, weakening the claim that the method is a principled causal intervention as opposed to an engineered reward shaping scheme dressed in causal language.

Computational cost is a material concern: computing sufficiency requires H continuations for each of T prefix positions per trajectory, i.e., O(T·H) generations per sample. The paper asserts this is 'manageable' via pre-collected offline rollouts, but a rigorous cost accounting or comparison of total wall-clock/compute versus baselines is missing beyond the qualitative Figure 12.

The empirical motivating analysis is qualitative only: gradient saliency maps over images (MLLM) are visually compared against token-embedding gradients (LLM), which are not directly commensurable quantities. No quantitative metric of background vs. foreground saliency or statistical evidence over a dataset is provided, so claim (i) in the abstract rests on a handful of illustrative examples.

Some reported results strain credibility and raise fairness questions: the method reportedly achieves state-of-the-art on essentially every benchmark, including 7B models beating GPT-4o and Qwen-VL-Max on V* and HR-Bench and outperforming tool-augmented systems like DeepEyes on refCOCO, ReasonSeg, and math benchmarks (Tables 5-7). It is unclear whether external baselines were reproduced under identical protocols or copied from original papers, and a hallucination-oriented reward explaining gains of +10-30 points on unrelated reasoning tasks is not convincingly analyzed.

The necessity intervention via masking a token to a zero/mask embedding changes the sequence in ways that are not equivalent to a do-intervention on the token variable; the paper does not discuss distribution shift between masked and sampled continuations, which affects the validity of the counterfactual interpretation.

Several technical details are under-specified or unclear: the relationship between the offline pre-collected rollouts and the evolving policy during training (risk of stale rewards), how the indicator-based sufficiency signal interacts with the group-normalized GRPO advantage, and the exact protocol for the GPT-4o-assisted evaluation.

Presentation issues: heavy notation with some redundant or awkwardly defined quantities (e.g., Eq. 3-4 for the token-level reward and KL), and the main text frequently defers essential details to the appendix, reducing readability of the core method.

strengths: Extensive empirical evaluation: hallucination benchmarks (CHAIR, POPE, GPT-4-assisted evaluation), text quality (MME), plus supplementary experiments on high-resolution understanding, grounding, and math/reasoning benchmarks, with comparisons to many recent baselines (DeCo, VTI, HA-DPO, CSR, GCPO, DeepEyes, etc.).

The motivating analysis (gradient saliency comparisons between a GRPO-trained MLLM and a text-only LLM, Figures 2 and 8) is a reasonable empirical hook, and the appendix provides additional qualitative examples and implementation detail (pseudo-code, notations, hyperparameters, H sensitivity).

The proposed token-level sufficiency/necessity reward is a concrete, implementable modification to GRPO, and ablations (Table 3, Table 9 on GRPO variants, Table 10 on reward application paths) support that the components contribute and that the reward composes with other GRPO-style methods.
Reproducibility is aided by pseudo-code, a notation table, implementation details, and a statement that code is provided in supplementary materials.
weaknesses: The causal formalization is shallow relative to the framing. The SCM in Figure 3 is largely decorative: L_c and L_s are never estimated or intervened on directly, and the 'sufficiency'/'necessity' scores are rollout-based heuristics (Eq. 6-7) closer to token-level credit assignment than to genuine PNS estimation. Related work [75] already applies sufficiency/necessity probing to CoT; the novelty is mainly moving this into a GRPO reward, which is an incremental step.

Technical soundness of the reward design is questionable. (i) Eq. 6 assigns S_suff = 0 whenever the indicator fails, conflating 'token does not improve answer' with 'token is not sufficient', and the indicator itself is noisy since r is computed from a finite number of stochastic rollouts. (ii) Necessity is estimated by masking a single token while retaining the rest of the sampled sequence; deleting one token rarely flips a correct answer, so most tokens should receive near-zero necessity, and the resulting distribution of r_causal (and its unnormalized addition to the advantage in Eq. 9) is never characterized statistically. (iii) Masked/mask-forced continuations are off-policy relative to the model, but no importance correction or analysis of this distribution mismatch is given.

The central causal claim — that outcome-only GRPO rewards actively induce spurious background reliance — is asserted from correlational saliency maps on a single model pair (LLaVA vs LLaMA) with qualitative examples; no intervention (e.g., ablating background, comparing reward designs on the same data) directly tests that the reward, rather than the visual modality or architecture, causes the effect.

Comparison fairness is mixed: many headline baselines (Beam Search, Nucleus, DoLa, OPERA, VCD, DeCo, VTI, CLIP-OHD) are training-free decoding or intervention methods, whereas COPO is a full RL fine-tuning of the same model, which can inflate apparent gains (Tables 1-2). Some fine-tuned baselines (CSR, GCPO, HA-DPO) are included, which helps, but the fine-tuning data and protocol for each baseline are not discussed.

Results on the supplementary extension (Qwen2.5-VL) strain credibility without supporting analysis: a hallucination-oriented reward yields large gains on V* Bench (+2.8), HR-Bench, refCOCO-type grounding, and six math benchmarks (Tables 5-7) simultaneously. This suggests either substantial confounds (e.g., the RL training data/recipe, which is under-specified — the dataset used for GRPO rollouts is never clearly stated) or evaluation procedures that need more scrutiny. SOTA-chasing across this many unrelated capability axes from a single hallucination reward is a red flag rather than a strength as presented.

The base models for the main experiments (InstructBLIP, MiniGPT-4, LLaVA-1.5, Qwen-VL) are dated for a 2026 submission, and limitations section acknowledges only scale (no 72B+ models) as a limitation.

Presentation has rough edges: heavy notation for a relatively simple reward, Eq. 5's P_sufficiency/P_necessity are defined but never actually estimated in the form given, hyperparameter interaction of lambda_s + lambda_n = 0.7 with the KL penalty and advantage scale is unanalyzed, and several figures are hard to parse at the reported level of detail.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem identification: the empirical analysis in Section 3.2 (gradient saliency concentrated on task-irrelevant background regions in MLLMs but not text-only LLMs under identical GRPO training) is a genuinely interesting observation that motivates the method, and it is supported by multiple scenarios in Figure 2 and Figure 8.

The proposed causal completeness reward is a reasonable and novel instantiation of token-level sufficiency/necessity constraints inside GRPO, and the paper is transparent about how it differs from closely related work (e.g., the discussion distinguishing COPO from causal probing methods [75] and causal-complete multimodal learning [63] in Appendix C.3).

Extensive empirical support: results span hallucination-specific metrics (CHAIR, POPE), text quality (MME, GPT-4o-assisted evaluation), high-resolution understanding, grounding, and math reasoning benchmarks, with consistent gains over a broad set of baselines including both training-free decoding methods and RL-based approaches (GCPO, POVID, CSR, HA-DPO).

Good ablation coverage: component ablations (Table 3), hyperparameter sensitivity for lambda_s, lambda_n (Figure 7) and H (Figure 11), decoding-mode comparisons (Table 8), plug-and-play integration with DAPO/Dr. GRPO/GCPO (Table 9), implementation-path variants (Table 10), and an efficiency trade-off analysis (Figure 12).
Reasonable reproducibility support: pseudo-code (Algorithms 1-2), a notation table, implementation details in Appendix G, and a statement that main code is provided in supplementary materials.
weaknesses: The causal framing is more rhetorical than formal. The SCM in Section 3.3 is not actually estimated or validated; the method ultimately reduces to counterfactual token ablation/masking for credit assignment. The connection between Eq. 5-8 and the PNS definition involves approximations (e.g., necessity is estimated with a single masked continuation while sufficiency averages H samples) whose bias is not analyzed.

The sufficiency score in Eq. 6 is gated by a hard indicator function, making the reward extremely sparse: tokens that do not strictly improve the expected outcome reward receive S_suff = 0 regardless of how close they are. The paper does not discuss how this sparsity interacts with advantage estimation or whether dense alternatives were tried.

Computational cost of token-level counterfactual estimation is substantial (H continuations per token per trajectory). The offline-rollout design in Appendix G mitigates this, but the paper does not report absolute training cost, and the trade-off analysis in Figure 12 uses a normalized, not clearly defined, cost axis.

The breadth of gains is under-explained: a method targeting hallucination yields SOTA on math reasoning (MathVision +2.3, WeMath +4.6), grounding (refCOCO series), and high-resolution benchmarks (Table 5-7), often over much larger or purpose-built systems (DeepEyes, ZoomEye). The mechanism by which suppressing background saliency produces these large general reasoning gains is not analyzed, and the training data used for GRPO fine-tuning is not clearly specified, which weakens both interpretability and reproducibility.

Baseline comparability is imperfect in Table 1: several baselines (OPERA, VCD, DeCo, DoLa, etc.) are training-free decoding interventions, whereas COPO involves fine-tuning; the fair comparison subset (GCPO, CSR, POVID) is present but the headline deltas conflate the two categories.

GPT-4o-assisted evaluation is based on only 100 images, and some evaluation protocols (e.g., the detailedness axis) may favor longer outputs that the causal reward could inadvertently encourage; variance or significance is not reported for any table.

Presentation issues: Eq. 9 states the hyperparameters also 'control the intensity of causal completeness rewards in the advantage,' which conflates reward weighting with advantage scaling and needs clearer treatment; several important details (training corpus, number of epochs) are deferred or missing.
